title: How AI Is Changing Legal Education with Dyane O'Leary and Jonah Perlin — full episode transcript
pub: AI and the Future of Law / 2030 Vision, American Arbitration Association
author: Dyane O'Leary · Jonah Perlin

dom.t: AI writing: Present gains can weaken future judgment

st.t: AI writing: Present gains can weaken future judgment
st.an: The source accepts supervised AI augmentation while materially extending the proposition with concrete assessment designs: AI-integrated instruction paired with face-to-face oral briefing and a closed-packet drafting exam to test independent understanding and writing competence. Its support is experiential and implementation-based, not evidence of measured learning outcomes.
qs: Now, they can use ChatGPT all they want to prep for that, but when it’s just me and them, face to face – sitting and talking through a problem with someone is a hard legal practice skill for today’s generation, but so valuable, because you can’t cheat it.

For instance, at Suffolk we’ve embraced AI – we’re integrating Hotshot’s legal AI modules into the first-year fall curriculum, we’re doing an exercise on AI outputs and prompting and all the things – but for the first time in a while, our students will take a closed-book legal writing final in December with just their brain, their fingertips, their laptop, and a closed packet of materials.

st.t: Service redesign: Resistance reflects incentives and identity
st.an: The source accepts that AI-driven change requires more than tool adoption and materially extends the cluster’s training and career-design dimension. It argues for adaptable, tool-agnostic AI education grounded in legal fundamentals, direct observation of practice and institutional constraints, while treating future task and career effects as uncertain rather than established.
qs: It feels totally right to me that unless our students have the background legal architecture and understand, you know, what is public law, what is private law, what are the sources of law, where do I go to find the sources of law to make sure their correct – the tools are not that useful to someone who’s going to use them as a lawyer, right?

So I think you should tell your stepdaughter and others: go see what lawyers do, try it on, see how it fits – but also try to build some of these tech skills that I think are going to be table stakes for the next generation of lawyers.

st.t: Supervised AI: Verification may consume efficiency gains
st.an: The source materially extends the cluster’s case against blanket AI-specific disclosure by showing that mandatory citation of complete prompt exchanges can be impractical and can itself expose confidential, privileged, or work-product material. It therefore supports contextual, lifecycle-aware disclosure controls rather than routine citation.
qs: So when we think about how cumbersome and unrealistic that is — for there to be a saved PDF screenshot of that entire exchange — that’s the practical yellow flag.
And the burden of combing through it — am I redacting parts of my citation for privilege?

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source accepts that AI’s effects are uneven and that legal work extends beyond automatable routine tasks, while materially extending the synthesis through concrete multimodal learning uses and professional-development guidance. It also adds a specific governance concern: comprehensive AI-exchange disclosure may create impractical recordkeeping, confidentiality and privilege risks.
qs: I had a student who told me she uploaded her Evidence outline and just engaged with it – quizzed herself on it, kind of used a chatbot as a tutor – which was amazing.
I think those of us who are really involved in the AI space sometimes forget that it hasn’t touched every aspect of lawyering.

st.t: AI instruction: Timing divides educational reform
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s central framing that legal education should develop AI competence alongside independently assessable legal skills. Perlin favors curriculum-wide integration, while O’Leary’s Suffolk example pairs first-year AI instruction with a closed-book writing final; the source also acknowledges disagreement over the timing and scope of AI access without offering comparative learning-outcome evidence.
qs: And frankly, I think I’m maybe in the minority, at least in my home institution, in believing that we need to integrate AI throughout the curriculum – in graded assignments and ungraded – in order to do this right.

For instance, at Suffolk we’ve embraced AI – we’re integrating Hotshot’s legal AI modules into the first-year fall curriculum, we’re doing an exercise on AI outputs and prompting and all the things – but for the first time in a while, our students will take a closed-book legal writing final in December with just their brain, their fingertips, their laptop, and a closed packet of materials.

st.t: Associate training: Automation threatens expertise reproduction
st.an: The source supports deliberate AI integration that preserves independent legal reasoning and direct practice exposure. Its concrete use of closed-book drafting and face-to-face oral assessment aligns with reconstructing training through independent practice and AI-critical workflows, while its evidence remains experiential rather than systematic.
qs: For instance, at Suffolk we’ve embraced AI – we’re integrating Hotshot’s legal AI modules into the first-year fall curriculum, we’re doing an exercise on AI outputs and prompting and all the things – but for the first time in a while, our students will take a closed-book legal writing final in December with just their brain, their fingertips, their laptop, and a closed packet of materials.

Now, they can use ChatGPT all they want to prep for that, but when it’s just me and them, face to face – sitting and talking through a problem with someone is a hard legal practice skill for today’s generation, but so valuable, because you can’t cheat it.

st.t: Expertise pipeline: Automated work weakens succession routes
st.an: The source accepts that AI may remove traditional junior-lawyer tasks while treating the result as a development and education challenge rather than straightforward replacement. It supports measured adaptation through AI fluency and broader professional judgment, while cautioning against reorganising legal education entirely around generative AI. Its claims are mainly predictions and anecdotes, consistent with the cluster’s emphasis on unresolved outcomes.
qs: There’s a lot of – I think, rightfully – concern that we’re going to lose all the tasks junior lawyers have traditionally done.
But I actually think there’s a real opportunity for junior lawyers to stand out in today’s legal organizations and law firms, because they are going to be more native in this technology.

st.t: Judgment development: AI exposure is not professional readiness
st.an: The source supports the distinction between AI exposure and professional readiness. It advocates curricular integration while insisting that personal familiarity or prompting fluency is not legal-workflow competence, and it pairs AI instruction with unaided assessment of students’ independent legal skills. Its claims are experiential rather than evidence of durable learning outcomes.
qs: But what I think every law student should know is that using these tools in their personal world (which is terrific, and as we’ve discussed, a great way to play and learn and get comfortable) is still not the same as using them in legal workflows.

For instance, at Suffolk we’ve embraced AI – we’re integrating Hotshot’s legal AI modules into the first-year fall curriculum, we’re doing an exercise on AI outputs and prompting and all the things – but for the first time in a while, our students will take a closed-book legal writing final in December with just their brain, their fingertips, their laptop, and a closed packet of materials.

st.t: Lawyer development: AI renews lifelong competence reform
st.an: The source directly supports preserving foundational legal reasoning while adapting legal education to technology-enabled practice. It advocates tool-agnostic learning skills, legal-source competence and some responsibility for practice readiness, while acknowledging institutional constraints and offering no comprehensive lifelong-development or funding model.
qs: But ultimately, the ability to think like a lawyer is going to become, I think, more important, not less important, in an AI-enhanced world.
I think it’s a good goal for them to be able to have those next-level conversations, but instead I think we need to give them the meta-skills of: How do I deal with a brand-new tool?

st.t: Practitioner engagement: Redesign should precede technological certainty
st.an: The source endorses practitioner-led experimentation through recurring classroom AI exercises while preserving broader legal education and humility. Its teaching examples are experiential and anecdotal rather than evidence of reliable outcomes, consistent with the cluster’s cautious reform agenda.
qs: My students start every week with “from the news” what stuck from the reading or video assigned and an “AI Aha!”.
We could redesign the entire three years of law school to focus on gen AI – but even saying that out loud, no, of course we shouldn’t do that.

st.t: Production model: Institutional absorption governs AI value
st.an: The source aligns with the cluster’s qualified account of AI adoption: AI is useful but fallible, legal education adapts slowly, and junior work may be displaced even as technological fluency creates new opportunities. It supports redesigned training and skills development while avoiding claims of proven sector-wide transformation.
qs: There’s a lot of – I think, rightfully – concern that we’re going to lose all the tasks junior lawyers have traditionally done.
But I actually think there’s a real opportunity for junior lawyers to stand out in today’s legal organizations and law firms, because they are going to be more native in this technology.

st.t: Selective augmentation: Verification constrains uneven productivity gains
st.an: The source aligns with selective augmentation: it presents AI as a useful but fallible thought partner while emphasizing higher-level lawyering, observation of real practice and humility about AI-driven curricular reform. Its evidence is anecdotal and it does not materially develop the cluster’s verification, productivity or staffing claims.
qs: If you’re serious about going into law as a profession, it’s maybe even more important now to see what’s beyond those tools.
Sometimes it gives me terrible outputs, but 99 times out of 100 it’s giving me really helpful, thought-provoking ideas.

st.t: Service model: AI challenges production more than lawyers
st.an: The source supports the proposition that AI’s present impact is concentrated in parts of legal production rather than eliminating the broader value of lawyers. It contrasts routine junior work with higher-level counselling, advocacy and trusted-adviser responsibilities, while stressing that AI adoption remains uneven and has not reached every area of practice.
qs: If you’re serious about going into law as a profession, it’s maybe even more important now to see what’s beyond those tools.
I think those of us who are really involved in the AI space sometimes forget that it hasn’t touched every aspect of lawyering.

kp.k: Professional AI use requires legal knowledge and workplace guidance
kp.d: O’Leary distinguishes students’ growing personal familiarity with AI from competence in legal workflows. Drawing on students’ accounts of internships and jobs, she reports uneven employer guidance, ranging from silence or unclear policies to substantial training. She recommends humility, legal foundations and a reusable set of questions about permitted tools and local policies; Perlin endorses this questioning capability.
qs: using these tools in their personal world (which is terrific, and as we’ve discussed, a great way to play and learn and get comfortable) is still not the same as using them in legal workflows.
What am I allowed to use? What’s the policy here? What’s the lay of the land?
the humility to know that you need a legal skill set to use these tools, and also knowing enough to ask what you don’t know

kp.k: Legal reasoning remains foundational; technological adaptability becomes essential
kp.d: Perlin argues that judgment, strategy, experience and reasoning will become more important in AI-enhanced practice, while the activities constituting legal practice change rapidly. Rather than teaching only current tools, he recommends meta-skills for learning unfamiliar technologies, linking these to future employer expectations and the Model Rules of Professional Conduct without identifying a specific rule.
qs: It’s our judgment, it’s our strategy, it’s our experience, it’s our reasoning.
ultimately, the ability to think like a lawyer is going to become, I think, more important, not less important, in an AI-enhanced world.
How do I deal with a tool that, by definition, didn’t exist when I went to law school? That’s what the Model Rules of Professional Conduct are going to require of future lawyers

kp.k: Workflow improvement becomes a new form of issue-spotting
kp.d: O’Leary recalls Suffolk’s dean describing innovation education over a decade earlier as issue-spotting for efficiency rather than only substantive legal issues. She applies this framework to tool-agnostic preparation: students should identify opportunities to improve delivery and save clients time or money, even while some still struggle with Word and Excel.
qs: Where can I spot new efficiencies here? Where can I find new ways to do this in a more efficient, effective way that saves my client money or time or improves my workflow?
Plenty of our students, frankly, are still struggling with using Word and Excel and all sorts of other tools.
our role as educators is maybe to plant the seed in a somewhat tool-agnostic way

kp.k: Assessment concerns can crowd out preparation for AI-enabled practice
kp.d: Perlin identifies grading and academic integrity as immediate institutional preoccupations that can subordinate practice-readiness discussions. He asserts, without presenting benchmark evidence, that AI can issue-spot almost as well as the average first-year student. He advocates integration across graded and ungraded work, while acknowledging disagreement and describing himself as possibly a minority at Georgetown on this question.
qs: I think the biggest challenge law schools are facing right now is they’re worried about how to deal with AI in the present in relation to how they grade students.
How do we do an issue-spotter exam where, frankly, an AI can issue-spot almost as well as the average 1L?
we need to integrate AI throughout the curriculum – in graded assignments and ungraded – in order to do this right.

kp.k: AI adoption concentrates in electives and legal writing
kp.d: O’Leary reports frequent requests from colleagues designing AI electives and experimentation across many legal writing programs, without quantifying adoption. Electives reach only some students, whereas legal writing offers a setting reaching all students. Despite these developments, she characterizes the doctrinal core as unchanged based on what she has seen over the last year or two.
qs: I have folks reach out to me probably every week who are designing a new AI elective for their law school
The other huge one is the legal writing course, which does reach all of your law students, and in an important way in a small setting.
We’re picking at the edges, but from my point of view, that core hasn’t changed at all.That’s what I’ve seen over the last year or two.

kp.k: Hybrid assessments combine AI practice with independent legal performance
kp.d: O’Leary describes balancing prompting, output evaluation and ethical instruction with oral briefings and closed-book writing to test students’ own understanding. Suffolk is integrating Hotshot’s legal AI modules into the first-year fall curriculum while planning a December legal writing final requiring drafting in three hours from a closed packet. She presents this balance as supporting both practice-readiness and bar preparation, not as a measured educational outcome.
qs: Yes, you might work with students on prompting and evaluating outputs and talk about the ethical use of AI. But then maybe two weeks later, you’re doing an oral exercise where they have to come into my office and brief me on a legal issue.
at Suffolk we’ve embraced AI – we’re integrating Hotshot’s legal AI modules into the first-year fall curriculum
They’ll have to draft something in three hours.
you need those critical thinking skills yourself to use these tools effectively.

kp.k: Classroom experiments illustrate statistical prediction, not legal accuracy
kp.d: In a 35-student upper-level elective involving 2Ls, 3Ls and 4L evening students, O’Leary had students use any tool to complete an unusual sentence and a summary-judgment sentence. She reports dispersed, associative answers to the former and more clustered legal answers to the latter, using the contrast to explain prediction and training-data relationships. This is a teaching anecdote, not a controlled comparison of model correctness.
qs: It’s a 35-student upper-level elective (2Ls, 3Ls and 4L evening students).
The alien ate the sandwich after the hockey game because …
The motion for summary judgment should be denied because …
the summary judgment ones, not remarkably, were much more bland and kind of clustered around the same output because the model had an easier time with that.

kp.k: AI can augment writing through simulated scholarly critique
kp.d: Perlin describes using basic ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini, rather than specialized legal models, as discussion partners for article drafts. He requests critique in particular scholars’ voices instead of generic improvement. He reports one instance in which later human feedback closely matched the simulation, explicitly calling it a sample size of one; his claim of helpful ideas 99 times out of 100 is a personal assessment, accompanied by acknowledgment of terrible outputs.
qs: Instead, I ask it to critique and offer advice in the mindset or voice of particular people.
I don’t know if that’s exactly the feedback those people would give
His feedback was almost exactly what the AI had predicted. And I was like, wow – sample size of one, but still, pretty wild!
Sometimes it gives me terrible outputs, but 99 times out of 100 it’s giving me really helpful, thought-provoking ideas.

kp.k: Junior task disruption may coexist with technology-driven career opportunities
kp.d: Perlin acknowledges some truth in concerns about losing traditional junior-lawyer tasks, but predicts opportunities for technologically fluent juniors to distinguish themselves and help organizations adapt. His supporting analogy is personal experience gaining case-team opportunities because he knew PowerPoint when partners did not, rather than evidence of AI-related hiring or displacement. He recommends retaining career observation while building technological skills.
qs: There’s a lot of – I think, rightfully – concern that we’re going to lose all the tasks junior lawyers have traditionally done. I think there’s some truth to that.
there’s a real opportunity for junior lawyers to stand out in today’s legal organizations and law firms, because they are going to be more native in this technology.
I got put on case teams and got to do things I never would have gotten to do based on my level of legal knowledge, simply because I could use a tool.
try to build some of these tech skills that I think are going to be table stakes for the next generation of lawyers.

kp.k: Career exploration should include higher-level counseling and courtroom practice
kp.d: O’Leary argues that observing entry-level document review has never adequately represented a legal career. She recommends that prospective students observe depositions, mediation, counseling and client crisis management, alongside courthouse practice. She cautions AI-focused observers against assuming universal transformation: in her account, substantial areas of lawyering remain available to observe without evident AI impact.
qs: If you’re serious about going into law as a profession, it’s maybe even more important now to see what’s beyond those tools.
What’s the higher-level counseling? How does someone become a trusted business advisor? What does it look like when a lawyer’s taking a call from a client in crisis?
I think those of us who are really involved in the AI space sometimes forget that it hasn’t touched every aspect of lawyering.

kp.k: Speakers differ on whether generative AI represents discontinuity
kp.d: O’Leary considers generative AI fundamentally different because it affects argument construction and substantive work product, unlike technologies she characterizes as primarily changing delivery processes. Perlin instead describes a natural progression, drawing analogies to natural-language research and the expansion of internet-related legal teaching. O’Leary clarifies the distinction between the law governing technology and technology used to deliver law, locating the strongest novelty in the latter.
qs: To me, this technology strikes more at the substance of lawyering. It really does – the words, the way we build our arguments, the essence of our work product.
I actually think this is a natural progression of tech change in lawyering.
there really are two lanes, and a lot of people conflate them: the technology of law, and the law of technology.
the “skills” bucket – the technology-of-law side – is where I see something really novel happening

kp.k: Bluebook AI citations raise practical and confidentiality concerns
kp.d: O’Leary criticizes new Bluebook Rule 18.3 for prescribing how to cite AI exchanges without resolving whether or when citation is appropriate. She describes screenshot preservation as cumbersome for iterative conversations and flags potential disclosure of client information, work product and privileged material. She situates these concerns in the difference between academic attribution norms and practice’s routine reuse of legal text; these are her interpretation and objections, not a quoted rule text.
qs: It just assumes one would be citing it.
gives a clunky citation format that has you saving screenshot captures of all your prompts.
Then there’s the ethical yellow flag: what’s in those prompts? Is there client information? Is that my work product? What are the potential ethical risks of disclosing it?
am I redacting parts of my citation for privilege?

kp.k: AI assists access to authority rather than constituting authority
kp.d: Both guests reject treating generated output as ordinary supporting legal authority. O’Leary plans to tell students that feeling a need to cite it probably signals misuse. Perlin offers a narrower reading of Rule 18.3: it could apply when an AI conversation itself is evidence in a dispute, rather than documenting how a brief was produced. He expects such use to be rare and explicitly presents this as his interpretation.
qs: It shouldn’t be a source that you feel like you need to cite to support your writing.
They’d need to cite that as an exhibit, right? Then they would use this rule on how to cite that chat.
This is not a rule about how you came up with your brief or your answer. We don’t cite junior associates. We don’t cite Google searches.
It’s a tool to get you to authority.

kp.k: Voice interaction expands drafting and personalized learning possibilities
kp.d: Perlin reports improved speech-to-text formatting and contrasts interactive AI with earlier dictation tools, suggesting renewed value in lawyers learning dictation. O’Leary supplies educational anecdotes: a student used an uploaded Evidence outline for conversational self-quizzing, and her class listened to a NotebookLM rendition of the syllabus. She sees potential for personalized academic support across modalities; no measured learning gains are reported.
qs: I’ve been so impressed by the ability now to just talk out an email and have it formatted properly, with names spelled correctly, and you don’t have to dictate your punctuation.
the old Dictaphone couldn’t talk back to you. And now the generative AI tools can talk back to you
I had a student who told me she uploaded her Evidence outline and just engaged with it – quizzed herself on it, kind of used a chatbot as a tutor
I had my students listen to my syllabus through Google’s NotebookLM as if it were a podcast

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: The interviewees anticipate changing legal workflows and training needs, while retaining foundational legal reasoning; they identify junior-lawyer opportunities, assessment challenges, and new writing and learning applications.
pts.d: Perlin predicts that legal judgment, strategy, experience and reasoning will become more important in an AI-enhanced profession, alongside adaptability to unfamiliar tools. O’Leary argues that personal familiarity with AI does not establish competence in legal workflows. Perlin acknowledges some truth in concerns about losing traditional junior-lawyer tasks, but predicts that technologically fluent juniors can gain opportunities within firms and other legal organizations. He also claims AI can already issue-spot almost as well as an average first-year law student, challenging conventional assessment. O’Leary reports growing AI electives and experimentation in legal writing, but says the doctrinal core remains unchanged. The interviewees differ on the character of the change: O’Leary sees AI as newly affecting the substance of legal work, whereas Perlin describes a natural progression of technological change. Perlin reports benefits from AI as a writing discussion partner and from improved speech-to-text and conversational interfaces; O’Leary describes multimodal tutoring applications. Both treat AI as a tool for reaching legal authority rather than as legal authority itself. O’Leary argues that Bluebook Rule 18.3's approach to preserving prompt exchanges is cumbersome and raises potential confidentiality and work-product concerns; Perlin interprets the rule as useful mainly in uncommon circumstances where the chat itself needs citation.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence offered is primarily teaching experience, personal experimentation, student reports and historical analogy, rather than systematic measurement.
pts.d: O’Leary draws on her 35-student upper-level elective, a classroom comparison of model sentence completions, reports from students about inconsistent workplace AI guidance, and contact with educators designing electives. She describes concrete Suffolk initiatives: Hotshot legal AI modules, prompting and output exercises, and a planned closed-book legal writing final. These illustrate curricular responses, rather than establish their effectiveness through measured outcomes. Perlin describes using general-purpose ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini for scholarly feedback, including one instance in which a scholar’s actual feedback closely matched AI-generated feedback. His '99 times out of 100' characterization is a personal assessment, not a reported benchmark. His junior-lawyer opportunity prediction draws partly on his own experience gaining assignments because he could use PowerPoint; no AI employment data are supplied. O’Leary offers a student’s self-quizzing with an Evidence outline and her own NotebookLM syllabus exercise as examples of multimodal learning. Perlin invokes the Model Rules of Professional Conduct and future employer expectations as reasons to teach adaptability, without identifying a particular rule. No benchmark is supplied for his comparison between AI and an average first-year student's issue-spotting, and no quantified evidence supports the broader labor-market predictions.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The discussion concerns current experience in 2025 and preparation for practice several years ahead; most broader predictions have no fixed deadline and depend on legal competence and workplace context.
pts.d: O’Leary emphasizes uncertainty about which tools students will encounter even today, much less in three or four years, and expects uneven workplace guidance to persist for a while. She reports curricular observations from the preceding year or two and describes Suffolk's December final as forthcoming. Perlin's junior-lawyer opportunity claim concerns current organizations and the next generation of lawyers, conditional on juniors having useful technological skills and intuition. Both regard independent legal reasoning as necessary for effective AI use, supporting a balance between AI-integrated instruction and unaided assessment. Perlin qualifies his scholarly-feedback example as a sample of one and does not claim the system reliably reproduces actual scholars' views. O’Leary says AI has not yet touched every aspect of lawyering, though she expects its reach to expand without specifying when. Perlin's expectation that Bluebook Rule 18.3 will be used rarely is explicitly tied to his interpretation of what the rule addresses.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The principal affected groups are law students, educators, junior lawyers and legal employers, with implications for clients, legal writers and learners using alternative modalities.
pts.d: For prospective and current law students, the interviewees emphasize learning substantive law, building technological adaptability and asking employers about permitted AI use. O’Leary distinguishes electives, which reach only some students, from required legal writing courses, which reach all students. Legal writing faculty and academic-support educators face new choices about instruction, tutoring, academic integrity and assessment. Junior lawyers may lose some traditional tasks but, in Perlin's account, gain access to opportunities through technological proficiency; he does not predict a quantified change in headcount. Firms and other employers must accommodate uneven capabilities and policies. O’Leary advises prospective students to observe higher-level counseling and client-facing judgment, while noting that some courtroom workflows remain untouched by AI. Clients may be affected by disclosure of sensitive information in cited prompt exchanges. Legal scholars and practitioners may benefit from AI-supported feedback, dictation and spoken interaction, while students may engage with course material through tutoring or audio formats. The source does not offer a distinct prediction about access to justice, ALSP market share or law-firm staffing ratios.
